gloss: A push or a pull that makes an object move, stop, or change shape.
examples: Gravity is the *force* that keeps us on the ground.
Two equal *forces* pulled the rope in opposite directions.
You have to apply more *force* to open that door.

gloss: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.
examples: The *mass* of the sample was exactly two grams.
*Mass* and weight are not the same thing.
The scientists compared the *masses* of the two particles.

gloss: How heavy something is.
examples: The nurse recorded my *weight* at every visit.
The shelf can't support that much *weight*.
*Weight* depends on gravity, but mass does not.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *wait*; the *gh* is silent.

gloss: How fast something moves.
examples: Light travels at a constant *speed* in a vacuum.
The car reached a *speed* of ninety miles an hour.
We measured the *speeds* of both marbles.

gloss: Speed in a particular direction.
examples: The rocket's *velocity* increased after the second burn.
In physics, *velocity* includes direction, but speed does not.
The two balls had equal but opposite *velocities*.

gloss: The rate at which something speeds up.
examples: This little car has surprising *acceleration*.
*Acceleration* is measured in meters per second squared.
The graph shows the *acceleration* over the first ten seconds.

gloss: The act or state of moving.
examples: Newton's laws describe the *motion* of objects.
The camera captures the *motion* of the bird's wings.
The bus was already in *motion* when he jumped off.

gloss: The force a moving object has because of its mass and its speed.
examples: A truck has far more *momentum* than a bicycle.
The sled lost *momentum* on the flat ground.
In a collision, the total *momentum* stays the same.

gloss: The force that slows down two surfaces rubbing against each other.
examples: *Friction* between the tires and the road slows the car.
Oil reduces the *friction* inside the engine.
Without *friction*, you couldn't walk across the floor.

gloss: The tendency of an object to keep doing whatever it is already doing.
examples: *Inertia* is why you lurch forward when the bus stops.
A heavy flywheel has a lot of *inertia*.
The seatbelt works against your body's *inertia*.

gloss: The turning force produced by an engine or applied to a bolt.
examples: This engine makes plenty of *torque* at low speeds.
Tighten each bolt to the *torque* listed in the manual.
A longer wrench gives you more *torque*.
contrast: Rhymes with *fork*; the *ue* is silent.

gloss: The pulling force in a stretched rope, wire, or spring.
examples: The cable snapped under the *tension*.
Adjust the *tension* on the belt before you start the motor.
*Tension* in the string keeps the weight from falling.

gloss: The forward force produced by an engine or a rocket.
examples: The engines produce enough *thrust* to lift the rocket.
The pilot cut the *thrust* just before landing.
Each booster adds *thrust* at liftoff.

gloss: The pressing of something into a smaller space.
examples: The *compression* of the gas raised its temperature.
Concrete is very strong under *compression*.
Low *compression* in one cylinder explains the misfire.

gloss: The amount of space between two points.
examples: Measure the *distance* between the two marks.
Sound travels long *distances* underwater.
At this *distance*, the star looks like a single dot.

gloss: How long something is from one end to the other.
examples: Record the *length* of each pendulum.
The two rods are exactly the same *length*.
We cut the wire into equal *lengths*.

gloss: How wide something is from side to side.
examples: Measure the *width* of the tray in centimeters.
The channel narrows to half its normal *width*.
The two strips have slightly different *widths*.

gloss: How tall something is, or how far it is above the ground.
examples: We dropped the ball from a *height* of two meters.
The balloon reached a *height* of ten thousand feet.
The two towers are almost the same *height*.
contrast: The *gh* is silent, and the word ends in *t*, not *th*.

gloss: How deep something is from the top down.
examples: The probe measured the *depth* of the lake.
At this *depth*, the pressure is enormous.
Samples were taken at three different *depths*.

gloss: The amount of flat surface that something covers.
examples: Calculate the *area* of the rectangle.
Pressure equals force divided by *area*.
The two shapes have equal *areas*.

gloss: The amount of space that something takes up.
examples: Pour the liquid in and read the *volume*.
The gas expands to fill the whole *volume*.
We compared the *volumes* of the two containers.

gloss: How much mass a material has for its size.
examples: Lead has a much higher *density* than aluminum.
Ice floats because its *density* is lower than water's.
The lab measured the *densities* of four metals.

gloss: An amount of something that can be counted or measured.
examples: Add a small *quantity* of acid to the beaker.
The plant gives off oxygen in large *quantities*.
Record both the *quantity* and the temperature.

gloss: A standard amount used for measuring, such as a meter or a gram.
examples: The meter is the standard *unit* of length.
Always write the *units* next to your answer.
Convert everything to the same *unit* first.

gloss: A number that you get by measuring something.
examples: Take three *measurements* and average them.
One *measurement* was clearly wrong.
Her *measurements* matched the published values.

gloss: A metric unit of length equal to about thirty-nine inches.
examples: The rope is exactly three *meters* long.
Light travels three hundred million *meters* per second.
Mark a line one *meter* from the wall.
contrast: American spelling *meter*; the British write *metre*.

gloss: A metric unit of mass equal to one thousandth of a kilogram.
examples: The sample weighed twelve *grams*.
Add one *gram* of salt to the water.
The scale reads to a tenth of a *gram*.

gloss: A metric unit of mass equal to one thousand grams.
examples: The package came in at just under two *kilograms*.
One liter of water has a mass of one *kilogram*.
The machine can lift fifty *kilograms*.

gloss: A unit for measuring electric current.
examples: This circuit is rated for fifteen *amps*.
The motor draws about two *amps*.
One *amp* is a lot of current for such a thin wire.

gloss: A unit for measuring the force that pushes an electric current.
examples: American outlets deliver a hundred and twenty *volts*.
The battery puts out nine *volts*.
A single *volt* won't hurt you.

gloss: A unit for measuring power.
examples: This bulb uses only nine *watts*.
The speaker is rated at fifty *watts*.
A microwave can draw a thousand *watts*.
contrast: For most Americans it sounds just like *what*.

gloss: A unit for measuring energy or work.
examples: Lifting the box took about ten *joules* of energy.
One calorie is roughly four *joules*.
The reading is given in *joules* per second.

gloss: A unit for measuring how many times something repeats each second.
examples: American house current runs at sixty *hertz*.
The tone was set to four hundred and forty *hertz*.
One *hertz* means one cycle per second.
contrast: The plural is also *hertz*, never *hertzes*.

gloss: A unit for measuring how loud a sound is.
examples: The machine runs at about seventy *decibels*.
A few extra *decibels* can damage your hearing.
Anything over a hundred and twenty *decibels* is painful.

gloss: The process of burning fuel together with oxygen.
examples: *Combustion* releases heat and carbon dioxide.
The engine runs on internal *combustion*.
Without oxygen, *combustion* stops immediately.

gloss: A sudden violent burst of energy that damages what is around it.
examples: The gas leak caused an *explosion*.
Two small *explosions* shook the building.
The *explosion* blew out every window on the street.

gloss: The hot glowing gas you see when something burns.
examples: Hold the wire in the *flame* until it glows.
The *flames* spread to the next room.
A blue *flame* means the gas is burning cleanly.

gloss: A tiny piece of burning material or a small flash of electricity.
examples: A single *spark* set off the whole fire.
*Sparks* flew when the metal hit the grinder.
The plug fires a *spark* on every cycle.

gloss: The change of a liquid into a gas.
examples: *Evaporation* cools your skin when you sweat.
The puddle disappeared through *evaporation*.
Cover the dish to prevent *evaporation*.

gloss: The change of a gas into a liquid, or the drops this leaves behind.
examples: *Condensation* formed on the cold glass.
Wipe the *condensation* off the window.
Clouds form by the *condensation* of water vapor.

gloss: The process of getting larger in size.
examples: Heat causes the *expansion* of most metals.
The bridge has gaps to allow for *expansion*.
The *expansion* of the gas pushed the piston out.

gloss: The process of getting smaller in size.
examples: Cooling leads to the *contraction* of the metal.
The rails leave room for *contraction* in winter.
*Contraction* pulled the seams apart.

gloss: The movement of heat through a liquid or gas as it circulates.
examples: This oven heats food by *convection*.
Warm air rises by *convection*.
*Convection* currents keep the water mixing.

gloss: Energy that travels out from a source as waves or particles.
examples: The lab shields its workers from *radiation*.
*Radiation* from the sun warms the earth.
They measured the *radiation* around the reactor.

gloss: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas.
examples: Water's *boiling point* is two hundred and twelve degrees Fahrenheit.
Alcohol has a lower *boiling point* than water.
The two liquids have very different *boiling points*.

gloss: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a solid.
examples: The *freezing point* of water is thirty-two degrees Fahrenheit.
Salt lowers the *freezing point* of water.
Different liquids have different *freezing points*.

gloss: The electrical force that pushes current through a circuit.
examples: Check the *voltage* before you plug it in.
High *voltage* can jump across a gap.
The two supplies run at different *voltages*.

gloss: How much a material slows down an electric current.
examples: Copper has very low *resistance*.
Measure the *resistance* across the two ends.
Higher *resistance* means less current.

gloss: A complete path that electricity can flow around.
examples: The *circuit* is broken somewhere near the switch.
Never work on a live *circuit*.
Both *circuits* are protected by fuses.
contrast: Spelled with *-uit*, but pronounced simply *-kit*.

gloss: A piece of metal that attracts iron and steel.
examples: Hold the *magnet* near the paper clips.
We stuck the drawing to the fridge with a *magnet*.
Two *magnets* will push apart if you flip one around.

gloss: The force by which magnets attract or push away other objects.
examples: *Magnetism* and electricity are closely related.
Heating the metal destroyed its *magnetism*.
The class covered *magnetism* last week.

gloss: A material that lets electricity or heat pass through it easily.
examples: Copper is an excellent *conductor*.
Water can act as a *conductor*, so be careful.
Metals are better *conductors* than plastics.

gloss: A material that does not let electricity or heat pass through.
examples: Rubber is a good *insulator*.
The handle is wrapped in an *insulator*.
Ceramic *insulators* hold the power lines away from the pole.

gloss: The thin wire inside a light bulb that glows when it heats up.
examples: The *filament* burned out after a year.
You can see the *filament* through the clear glass.
Old bulbs used tungsten *filaments*.

gloss: A device that raises or lowers the voltage of an electric supply.
examples: The *transformer* on the pole blew during the storm.
A small *transformer* steps the voltage down to twelve volts.
Both *transformers* were replaced last year.

gloss: The distance from one wave to the next one.
examples: Red light has a longer *wavelength* than blue light.
The antenna is tuned to that *wavelength*.
Different *wavelengths* bend by different amounts.

gloss: The number of times a wave or an event repeats each second.
examples: Raise the *frequency* and the pitch goes up.
The radio picks up several *frequencies*.
A high *frequency* means a short wavelength.

gloss: A fast shaking movement back and forth.
examples: You can feel the *vibration* through the floor.
*Vibrations* from the engine loosened the bolt.
Rubber pads absorb most of the *vibration*.

gloss: Light or sound bouncing back from a surface, or the image this makes.
examples: She saw her *reflection* in the store window.
The *reflection* off the water was blinding.
We measured the *reflections* of sound in the empty hall.

gloss: The bending of light as it passes from one material into another.
examples: *Refraction* makes the straw look broken in the glass.
A lens works by *refraction*.
*Refraction* in the atmosphere shifts the star's position slightly.

gloss: A clear block of glass that splits light into colors.
examples: Hold the *prism* up in the sunlight.
The *prism* spread the beam into a rainbow.
Two glass *prisms* sat on the lab bench.

gloss: A device that produces a narrow, very bright beam of light.
examples: The *laser* cuts right through sheet metal.
Don't point the *laser* at anyone's eyes.
Surgeons use *lasers* for some eye operations.

gloss: An instrument that makes very small things look much bigger.
examples: Put the slide under the *microscope*.
You can see bacteria through a good *microscope*.
The lab has six *microscopes*.

gloss: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
examples: Solids, liquids, and gases are all forms of *matter*.
*Matter* cannot be created or destroyed.
The telescope detects *matter* falling into the black hole.

gloss: A substance that keeps its own shape, such as ice or wood.
examples: Ice is water in the form of a *solid*.
*Solids* usually expand a little when they are heated.
The mixture separates into a *solid* and a liquid.

gloss: One of the forms that matter can take, or one stage of a process.
examples: Water has three *phases*: solid, liquid, and gas.
The metal changes *phase* at that temperature.
We are still in the first *phase* of the experiment.

gloss: A very hot gas whose particles carry an electric charge.
examples: Stars are made of *plasma*.
The lamp glows because the gas turns into *plasma*.
*Plasma* is often called the fourth state of matter.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid or gas that flows and takes the shape of its container.
examples: Brake *fluid* should be changed every few years.
Both gases and liquids are *fluids*.
The pump moves *fluid* through the pipes.

gloss: The smallest unit of a chemical element.
examples: A water molecule contains three *atoms*.
Every *atom* has a nucleus at its center.
The scientists managed to split the *atom*.

gloss: A group of atoms joined together, the smallest piece of a compound.
examples: A water *molecule* is two hydrogens and one oxygen.
*Molecules* move faster when you heat them.
The drug attaches to one *molecule* at a time.

gloss: A tiny particle with a negative charge that moves around an atom.
examples: Electric current is a flow of *electrons*.
An *electron* is far lighter than a proton.
This metal gives up one *electron* easily.

gloss: A particle with a positive charge found in the center of an atom.
examples: Each *proton* carries a positive charge.
Carbon has six *protons*.
The number of *protons* decides which element it is.

gloss: A particle with no electric charge found in the center of an atom.
examples: A *neutron* weighs about the same as a proton.
The nucleus holds both protons and *neutrons*.
Free *neutrons* keep the reaction going.

gloss: An extremely small piece of matter.
examples: Dust *particles* floated in the sunlight.
The filter traps any *particle* larger than a micron.
Physicists study how one *particle* hits another.

gloss: An atom that carries an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
examples: Salt splits into two *ions* when it dissolves.
A sodium *ion* has a positive charge.
The *ions* carry the current through the liquid.
contrast: Not the same word as *iron*, which is EYE-urn.

gloss: A form of an element that has a different number of neutrons.
examples: Carbon has several *isotopes*.
One *isotope* of hydrogen is used in reactors.
Doctors use a radioactive *isotope* to trace blood flow.

gloss: A metal made by mixing two or more metals together.
examples: Brass is an *alloy* of copper and zinc.
The frame is made from a light aluminum *alloy*.
Different *alloys* melt at different temperatures.
contrast: The noun is AL-oy; the rare verb is uh-LOY.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid with something dissolved in it.
examples: Pour the salt *solution* into the beaker.
Prepare two *solutions* of different strength.
The *solution* turned blue when we added the powder.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid that can dissolve other substances.
examples: Water is the most common *solvent* of all.
Use a *solvent* to get the paint off.
Some *solvents* give off dangerous fumes.

gloss: A chemical substance that neutralizes an acid.
examples: Baking soda is a mild *base*.
An acid and a *base* react to make salt and water.
Strong *bases* can burn your skin.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *bass*, the low musical sound.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A compound formed when a substance combines with oxygen.
examples: Rust is an *oxide* of iron.
The white powder is zinc *oxide*.
Several *oxides* formed on the surface.

gloss: A compound of chlorine with another element, such as table salt.
examples: Table salt is sodium *chloride*.
The well water contains too much *chloride*.
*Chloride* levels in the sample were high.

gloss: A material made of very long chains of repeating molecules.
examples: Most plastics are *polymers*.
The coating is a flexible *polymer*.
New *polymers* are replacing metal parts.

gloss: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
examples: The reaction needs a *catalyst* to go quickly.
Platinum acts as a *catalyst* in the exhaust system.
Enzymes are biological *catalysts*.

gloss: A substance made by living cells that speeds up a chemical reaction.
examples: This *enzyme* breaks down starch.
Digestive *enzymes* work best at body temperature.
Heat destroys the *enzyme*.

gloss: How much of a substance is present in a mixture.
examples: Increase the *concentration* of the acid slightly.
High *concentrations* of salt kill the plants.
The *concentration* dropped as we added water.

gloss: How acid something is.
examples: Test the *acidity* of the soil before planting.
Lemon juice adds *acidity* to the sauce.
The *acidity* of the rain has damaged the stone.

gloss: How thick a liquid is and how slowly it flows.
examples: Honey has a very high *viscosity*.
Cold weather increases the oil's *viscosity*.
We measured the *viscosity* at three temperatures.

gloss: How free a substance is from other materials mixed into it.
examples: The lab checks the *purity* of every batch.
Gold is sold by weight and *purity*.
A *purity* above ninety-nine percent is required.

gloss: How well a material carries electricity or heat.
examples: Silver has the highest electrical *conductivity* of any metal.
Salt raises the water's *conductivity*.
We measured the *conductivity* of each sample.

gloss: A process in which substances change into different substances.
examples: The *reaction* gives off a lot of heat.
Some *reactions* will not start without a catalyst.
Mixing the two powders starts the *reaction*.

gloss: A reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen.
examples: Rust is caused by *oxidation*.
The coating slows the *oxidation* of the metal.
*Oxidation* is what turns a cut apple brown.

gloss: The slow damage caused when a metal reacts with air or water.
examples: Salt on the roads speeds up *corrosion*.
There was heavy *corrosion* around the battery terminals.
Paint protects the steel from *corrosion*.

gloss: The gradual breaking down of a substance or of a radioactive material.
examples: Radioactive *decay* releases energy over time.
The rate of *decay* is measured in half-lives.
Bacteria cause *decay* in dead plants.

gloss: The splitting of an atom's nucleus, which releases energy.
examples: Nuclear *fission* powers the plant.
The *fission* of uranium releases enormous energy.
The reactor controls the rate of *fission*.

gloss: The joining of two atomic nuclei, which releases a huge amount of energy.
examples: The sun is powered by *fusion*.
*Fusion* would give us almost limitless energy.
Scientists have struggled for decades to control *fusion*.

gloss: A large machine in which nuclear reactions are controlled to make energy.
examples: The *reactor* was shut down for maintenance.
Two *reactors* supply the whole city.
Water cools the core of the *reactor*.

gloss: A very light gas that is used to fill balloons.
examples: The balloons are filled with *helium*.
*Helium* makes your voice sound funny.
There is a worldwide shortage of *helium*.

gloss: A greenish gas used to kill germs in water.
examples: The pool smells strongly of *chlorine*.
*Chlorine* is added to drinking water.
Too much *chlorine* irritates your eyes.

gloss: A soft silver-white metal that is one half of ordinary salt.
examples: The label lists the amount of *sodium* per serving.
*Sodium* reacts violently with water.
Cut back on *sodium* if your blood pressure is high.

gloss: A silver-white metal found in bones, teeth, and milk.
examples: Milk is a good source of *calcium*.
Her doctor told her to take more *calcium*.
*Calcium* builds up inside the pipes.

gloss: A soft silver-white metal that the body needs in small amounts.
examples: Bananas contain a lot of *potassium*.
Low *potassium* can cause muscle cramps.
The fertilizer supplies nitrogen and *potassium*.

gloss: A light silver-white metal that burns with a bright white flame.
examples: *Magnesium* burns with a blinding white light.
The frame is made of a *magnesium* alloy.
She takes *magnesium* for her leg cramps.

gloss: A heavy radioactive metal used as nuclear fuel.
examples: The plant runs on enriched *uranium*.
*Uranium* is mined in several western states.
They found traces of *uranium* in the soil.

gloss: A soft black form of carbon used in pencils.
examples: Pencil leads are made of *graphite* and clay.
*Graphite* conducts electricity.
The rods are coated with *graphite*.

gloss: The thick oil taken from underground and refined into fuel.
examples: Gasoline is made from *petroleum*.
*Petroleum* prices rose again this month.
Most plastics are a *petroleum* product.

gloss: The gray powder that is left after something has burned.
examples: There was *ash* all over the grill.
Volcanic *ash* closed the airport for two days.
Sweep the *ash* out of the fireplace.
contrast: *Ashes* is a separate word, used for the remains of a fire or a body.

gloss: The fine black powder left behind by smoke.
examples: The chimney was black with *soot*.
*Soot* had settled on every surface in the room.
He wiped the *soot* off the glass.
contrast: Rhymes with *foot*, not with *suit*.

gloss: A small amount of something left behind after a process.
examples: A sticky *residue* stayed on the glass.
Wash off any *residue* before you weigh it.
Pesticide *residues* were found on the fruit.

gloss: Solid material that settles at the bottom of a liquid.
examples: *Sediment* collected at the bottom of the tube.
The river carries *sediment* downstream.
Pour it off slowly and leave the *sediment* behind.

gloss: A room or building where scientific work is done.
examples: The samples went straight to the *laboratory*.
She runs a research *laboratory* at the university.
Both *laboratories* got the same result.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, LAB-ruh-tor-ee; the British say luh-BOR-uh-tree.

gloss: An informal word for a laboratory.
examples: We ran the test in the *lab*.
Her *lab* is on the third floor.
Most of the *labs* close at six.

gloss: A thin glass tube closed at one end, used for experiments.
examples: Pour the acid into a clean *test tube*.
Hold the *test tube* with tongs, not with your fingers.
A rack of *test tubes* sat on the bench.

gloss: A wide glass cup with a lip, used for mixing liquids in a lab.
examples: Fill the *beaker* to the hundred-milliliter mark.
The liquid in the *beaker* turned pink.
Wash the *beakers* before you leave.

gloss: A thin tube used to move an exact amount of liquid.
examples: Use a *pipette* to add exactly five milliliters.
Rinse the *pipette* between samples.
The *pipettes* are in the top drawer.

gloss: A cone-shaped tube used for pouring liquid into a narrow opening.
examples: Use a *funnel* so you don't spill it.
The *funnel* was lined with filter paper.
Two plastic *funnels* hung by the sink.

gloss: A small tube with a rubber bulb for releasing liquid one drop at a time.
examples: Add the dye with a *dropper*.
The *dropper* holds about a milliliter.
Both *droppers* were labeled with tape.

gloss: A plug of rubber, glass, or cork that closes a bottle or a tube.
examples: Push the *stopper* firmly into the flask.
The *stopper* popped out from the pressure.
Rubber *stoppers* come in several sizes.

gloss: A tube-shaped object or container with flat circular ends.
examples: Measure the volume in a graduated *cylinder*.
The gas comes in a heavy steel *cylinder*.
This engine has four *cylinders*.

gloss: A device that removes solid pieces or unwanted material from a liquid or gas.
examples: Pour the mixture through a paper *filter*.
Change the air *filter* once a year.
The *filters* clogged after an hour.

gloss: A very thin layer that lets some substances pass through it.
examples: Water passes through the *membrane* but salt does not.
The *membrane* tore under the pressure.
Cell *membranes* control what goes in and out.

gloss: A thin instrument used to measure or examine something.
examples: Insert the temperature *probe* into the sample.
The *probe* sends data back every second.
Two *probes* recorded the voltage.

gloss: A device that detects heat, light, motion, or another physical change.
examples: The *sensor* switches the light on automatically.
A faulty *sensor* gave us the wrong reading.
*Sensors* on the bridge measure the strain.

gloss: A device that finds the presence of something such as smoke or radiation.
examples: The smoke *detector* went off at midnight.
The metal *detector* beeped at his belt buckle.
Radiation *detectors* line the corridor.

gloss: A watch used to time something exactly.
examples: Start the *stopwatch* when the ball is released.
The coach clicked the *stopwatch* at the finish line.
Both *stopwatches* showed the same time.

gloss: An instrument with a magnetic needle that shows which way is north.
examples: The needle of the *compass* swung toward the magnet.
Take a *compass* if you're hiking off the trail.
The old brass *compasses* still work perfectly.

gloss: A tool used for careful scientific work or measurement.
examples: Every *instrument* in the lab is calibrated once a year.
The *instrument* measures pressure to four decimal places.
Delicate *instruments* must be handled carefully.

gloss: A machine that turns fuel or electricity into movement.
examples: The *engine* burns a mixture of fuel and air.
Both *engines* shut down at the same moment.
A diesel *engine* is more efficient than a gasoline one.

gloss: A machine with blades that spin to produce power.
examples: Steam drives the *turbine*.
Wind *turbines* line the whole ridge.
The *turbine* generates enough power for a small town.

gloss: A part that slides up and down inside a cylinder to create movement.
examples: The *piston* moves down as the gas expands.
One *piston* was badly scratched.
This engine has six *pistons*.

gloss: A scientific test done to find out whether an idea is true.
examples: The *experiment* took three weeks.
We repeated the *experiment* twice to be sure.
Her *experiments* changed how we think about heat.

gloss: A procedure done to find out what something is or how well it works.
examples: The lab ran a *test* on the water sample.
Both *tests* came back negative.
We put the new material through a strength *test*.

gloss: One run of an experiment or test.
examples: The drug is still in clinical *trials*.
Each *trial* gave a slightly different number.
We averaged the results of ten *trials*.

gloss: A small amount of something taken to be examined or tested.
examples: Take a *sample* of the water from the tap.
The *samples* are stored in a freezer.
Each *sample* was labeled with a date.

gloss: A single item or piece taken as an example for study.
examples: The museum has a rare *specimen* of that mineral.
Label each *specimen* clearly.
The *specimen* was mounted on a glass slide.
contrast: Stress the first syllable: SPES-uh-muhn.

gloss: Something you notice and write down while watching carefully.
examples: Write your *observations* in the notebook.
One *observation* did not fit the pattern.
The theory rests on years of careful *observations*.

gloss: What you find out at the end of an experiment or test.
examples: The *results* surprised everyone in the lab.
We got the same *result* three times in a row.
Her *results* were published last spring.

gloss: Facts and numbers collected for study.
examples: The *data* shows a clear trend.
We collected *data* for six months.
All of the *data* is stored on the server.
contrast: In American English *data* normally takes a singular verb: *the data is*.

gloss: A set of ideas that explains why something happens.
examples: Einstein's *theory* changed physics forever.
There are several competing *theories*.
The *theory* predicts exactly what we measured.

gloss: A basic scientific rule that explains how something works.
examples: The pump works on a very simple *principle*.
He explained the *principle* behind the experiment.
The same *principles* apply to gases and liquids.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *principal*, the head of a school.

gloss: A mathematical statement that two amounts are equal.
examples: Solve the *equation* for the unknown value.
The *equation* balances on both sides.
These *equations* describe how the wave moves.
contrast: The ending is -ZHUHN, not -SHUHN.

gloss: A planned way of doing something.
examples: The scientific *method* starts with a question.
We tried a different *method* the second time.
Both *methods* gave the same answer.

gloss: The set of steps you follow to do something correctly.
examples: Follow the safety *procedure* exactly.
The whole *procedure* takes about twenty minutes.
Lab *procedures* are posted on the wall.

gloss: A particular skilled way of doing something.
examples: The new *technique* saves hours of work.
She developed a *technique* for growing the crystals.
Both *techniques* have their drawbacks.
contrast: The *-que* ending is just a *k* sound: tek-NEEK.

gloss: Something in an experiment that can change.
examples: Change only one *variable* at a time.
Temperature was the one *variable* we controlled.
Too many *variables* make the results hard to read.

gloss: A drawing that shows how two sets of numbers are related.
examples: Plot your results on a *graph*.
The *graph* shows a steady rise.
Both *graphs* use the same scale.
contrast: The *ph* is pronounced like *f*.

gloss: A simple drawing that explains how something works or is arranged.
examples: Label every part of the *diagram*.
The *diagram* shows the flow of current.
The manual has *diagrams* for each step.

gloss: The science of what substances are made of and how they react.
examples: She teaches *chemistry* at the high school.
*Chemistry* was my favorite subject.
The *chemistry* behind the reaction is simple.
contrast: The *ch* is pronounced like *k*.

gloss: A scientist who studies chemical substances and reactions.
examples: A *chemist* analyzed the sample for us.
*Chemists* developed the new coating.
He worked as a *chemist* for a paint company.
contrast: In America a *chemist* is a scientist; in Britain the word can also mean a pharmacist.

gloss: A scientist who studies matter, energy, and forces.
examples: The *physicist* explained the results to the reporters.
Several *physicists* worked on the design.
She trained as a *physicist* before switching to medicine.
contrast: Stress the first syllable: FIZ-uh-sist.
